The Red-chested swallow Cecropis semirufa is a medium-sized hirundine widely distributed across sub-Saharan Africa, where it occupies open savannas and cultivated landscapes. Eggs incubated at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] typically hatch after a period of 19.5 days [ab = 19.5 days], a value consistent with the incubation durations documented for other tropical members of the genus. Upon hatching, the altricial nestlings emerge at a remarkably low wet weight at birth of 2.2 grams [Wwb = 2.2 grams], representing a modest fraction of the eventual adult mass. This initial mass is comparable to that reported for the closely related barn swallow Hirundo rustica (2.2 grams) [Wwb = 2.2 grams], reflecting the conservative pattern of yolk investment characteristic of aerial insectivores. The rapid growth trajectory that follows is fueled by intensive biparental provisioning, with both adults delivering insect prey to the developing chicks throughout the daylight hours. The nestling period is energetically demanding, requiring sustained food delivery to support the accelerated tissue deposition that underpins feather development and mass gain.

Under the standard thermal conditions that define the species' active metabolic period during the breeding season (41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]), a predictable sequence of developmental milestones unfolds. The transition to independence begins with fledging, which occurs at 26 days since birth [tx = 26 days since birth], although the typical range reported in field studies extends from 18 to 23 days depending on local resource availability and brood size at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively short nestling stage is characteristic of open-cup nesting hirundines that face elevated predation risk, favoring an early departure from the nest despite incomplete flight feather maturation. Following fledging, the juveniles remain dependent on parental feeding for an additional period while refining their aerial foraging skills. The timing of fledging is tightly coupled with the attainment of a critical body mass threshold that ensures sufficient energy reserves to support the initial days of independent flight and exploration.

Sexual maturation in this species follows a distinct developmental schedule that is similarly assessed at the metabolically relevant temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Puberty, marking the onset of gonadal activity and the capacity to produce gametes, is reached at 78 days since birth [tp = 78 days since birth], a value that aligns with the lower bound of the 18 to 23 day range sometimes cited for the initiation of reproductive physiology in related species at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively rapid progression to sexual maturity reflects the selective pressures of a seasonally variable environment where early breeding can confer a significant advantage in terms of lifetime reproductive output. The attainment of puberty does not, however, immediately translate into successful breeding, as individuals must also acquire territories and secure sufficient foraging resources. The 78-day figure represents the physiological capability rather than the ecological realization of reproduction, and field observations indicate that many yearlings defer actual nesting until their second calendar year.

The age at first successful reproduction, or the time since birth at first brood, is a critical life-history parameter that integrates both physiological readiness and ecological opportunity. Under the thermal regime of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], first broods are typically initiated at 365 days since birth [tR = 365 days since birth], corresponding to the onset of the first full breeding season following the individual's birth. This delay between puberty and first reproduction is common among hirundines and is interpreted as a consequence of the substantial energetic demands of nest construction, egg production, and the prolonged provisioning of altricial young. The 365-day interval ensures that individuals have completed a full cycle of feather replacement and have accumulated sufficient lipid reserves to support the reproductive effort without compromising their own survival probability. Comparative data from long-term population studies suggest that this reproductive delay enhances overall lifetime fitness by reducing the mortality risk associated with first-time breeding.

The initial wet weight of the freshly laid egg is approximately 2.9 grams [Ww0 = approximately 2.9 grams], a value that reflects the moderate investment typical of aerial insectivores. Adult body mass provides a fundamental index of somatic condition and energetic status in these birds. The ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown adult Red-chested swallows is approximately 30.9 grams [Wwi = approximately 30.9 grams], placing them among the mid-sized members of the genus Cecropis. Females produce clutches of 3 to 4 eggs [N_R_i = clutches of 3 to 4 eggs] and typically raise two broods annually [F_R_i = two broods annually], a reproductive rate that balances the high per-offspring investment with the opportunity for multiple nesting attempts within a single season. This relatively modest clutch size is thought to reflect the constraints imposed by the energetic demands of sustained aerial foraging and the elevated predation risk associated with open-cup nesting in savanna habitats. In the absence of a direct longevity record for Cecropis semirufa, maximum lifespan is estimated at approximately 16 years [am = approximately 16 years], based on the closely related barn swallow Hirundo rustica at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C].
